rejected.title: Proof with vectors
card: Set up a shape using vectors from one origin O. The position vector of a point P is OP. For a parallelogram OABC, let a = OA and c = OC. Then OB = a + c, because B is reached by going along OA and then along OC.
Opposite sides of a parallelogram are parallel and equal in length, so AB = OC = c and CB = OA = a.
To show the diagonals bisect each other, find the midpoint of each diagonal. The midpoint of OB is ½(a + c). The diagonal AC = c − a, so the midpoint of AC is a + ½(c − a) = ½(a + c).
Both midpoints have the same position vector, so they are the same point. The diagonals cross at their midpoints, so they bisect each other.
rejected.remember: Write each point as a vector from one origin, then show two routes give the same vector.

a.q: In parallelogram OABC, a = OA and c = OC. Which vector is the diagonal OB?
a.why: B is reached by going along OA and then along OC, so OB = a + c. The vector c − a is the other diagonal AC, and ½(a + c) is only the midpoint of OB.
a.clue: Go from O to A, then from A to B.

b.q: In parallelogram OABC, a = OA and c = OC. M is the midpoint of side AB. What is the position vector of M?
b.why: Start at A, then go half of AB, which equals c: OM = a + ½c. The vector ½(a + c) is where the diagonals meet, not the midpoint of side AB. Using ½c alone leaves out the start at A.
b.clue: Start at A, then add half of the vector AB.

b.q: In parallelogram OABC, a = OA and c = OC. Which working shows the midpoint of diagonal AC has position vector ½(a + c)?
b.why: AC = c − a, so the midpoint is a plus half of AC: a + ½(c − a) = ½(a + c). Using a − c reverses the direction of AC. Leaving out the starting vector a gives only half of AC, not a position vector.
b.clue: Start at A, then add half of the vector AC.
